fact_reason: 'In Mexico we call it the Mexican wave' (and the Argentine family 'said the same thing'). In Mexico and other Spanish-speaking countries it is called 'la ola'; 'Mexican wave' is the name used by English speakers outside North America (source: Wikipedia, Wave (audience)).

fact_reason: "The one closest to the slide," Nevaeh said, for the lowest-power lens. The low-power objective is the shortest and sits farthest from the slide; the high-power objective is longest and comes closest (umdearborn.edu microscope guide / Pearson microscopy study guide).

fact_reason: 'Sahara. Arabian. Kalahari. Australian outback. Atacaca.' The desert is the Atacama; 'Atacaca' is a wrong place name. The 30-degree belts and the sinking-air explanation are correct.

'He was always drawing the sides of buildings straight up and down, but the print was telling him the lines should slant toward one invisible target.' In one-point perspective vertical edges stay vertical; only lines receding into depth converge on the vanishing point.

fact_reason: 'The problem, he decided, was the order of the colors ... The second one blurred into something smoother, less brown.' fact_reason: 'if his dad had stopped growing at fourteen, and his uncle at seventeen, then the family plates closed late... Late closers, all of them.' A boy who stops growing at 14 has growth plates that closed early, not late, so the story endorses a wrong conclusion about growth.

fact_reason: 'Forty-two minus three is 39, but my total says 38.' The worked SUM logic treats every cell as 1 (SUM of the vote column equals the ballot count) while a text cell holds '3; dropping it would lower the sum by 3, so the arithmetic and the SUM-as-count idea are wrong.

'You're not slower. You were just measured in a different pool.' Long-course (50 m) times are slower than short-course yard times because of fewer turns, so if Priya's summer long-course time was faster than her 25-yard tryout time she really did get slower (source: SwimTopia 'Converting Swim Times', USMS forum).

fact_reason: 'he borrowed a ten from the five's place, made it fourteen, and it came out two dollars and thirty-five cents.' No digit becomes fourteen when subtracting 2.65 from 5.00; regrouping gives 4 dollars, 9 dimes, 10 cents (10-5, 9-6, 4-2 = 2.35).

fact_reason: 'Dex laid it in off the glass, no rim, nothing but net.' 'Nothing but net' means the ball goes through without touching the rim or backboard (dummies.com basketball terms), so a shot off the glass cannot be nothing but net.

fact_reason: 'There's a winter league with January tryouts. New year, new cutoff. I'll be the old one for once.' With a January 1 cutoff a December-born player stays the youngest in his birth-year group whenever tryouts are held; the relative age effect depends on birth date relative to the cutoff, not on tryout timing.

'One hand, no weight on the broken side' — the story shows a child with a broken arm in a cast hanging from the monkey bars and frames it as sensible. Children's Wisconsin orthopedic guidance says to avoid monkey bars even for 2 weeks after the cast comes off; hanging one-handed while still in a cast is unsafe.

fact_reason: 'So the blockage was puffy, swollen walls, not a pile of gunk' and 'It's not a mucus problem.' The fact says swelling is the main cause, not the only one; mucus also contributes.

fact_reason: 'It says best if used by. Not use by.' / calling out 'quality date' or 'safety date'. USDA FSIS says a 'Use-By' date is also a peak-quality date and not a safety date except on infant formula (source: FSIS 'Food Product Dating').
'Him: 10 for 27, which turned into 38 percent.' 10 divided by 27 is 37.0 percent, not 38 percent. Kayla's 5 for 11 = 45 percent is correct.

'the machine replied "not prime" for every divisor it tested: 7 printed "not prime," then 7 again... One number in, fifty lines out.' Between 2 and 48, 49 has only one divisor (7), so a loop that prints only when a divisor divides evenly prints "not prime" once, not fifty times.
